<reason>Both sides were strong and format-compliant (proper Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 throughout, no fake precision). B had the flashier material — the orchestra analogy, the arbiter fork, and a memorable closing ("a claim to litigate, or a job to take") — and B's enforcement critique genuinely damaged A's case: A's layered-arbiter answer leans on unions, existing accommodation law, and courts, which B fairly reduced. But B's signature attack overreached: claiming the motion's distinction "dies" because role reasons reference other people conflates relational reasons with broad culture assertions, and A repeatedly showed the operative difference — "senior analysts Tue–Thu for live case reviews" is checkable and schedulable while "culture demands five days" is not. B never squarely answered that falsifiability asymmetry, mostly restating the equivalence. A also won the distributional weighing: B's market alternative works through exit, and A's point that the single parent pays first and becomes attrition data was turned but not neutralized, especially for incumbents in concentrated markets. B's late "padded mandate" point misdescribes A's standard, which from the opening required justifying frequency as well as presence. A kept the debate on the motion as written and exited with more intact routes to victory.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The three-round fight over the orchestra analogy: A2.1 flipped it (the violinist cites timing and cues, not vibes), B2.1/B4.2 countered that this concedes the network and kills the distinction, but A4.2's "choreography, not fog" — who needs whom, when, for what task — held because B never explained why such a claim cannot be written or checked role-by-role.</best_rebuttal>
